newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli foreign currency borrowing rose in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Israeli foreign currency borrowing rose in 1996.

text.p: Israeli banks' shekel loans linked to foreign currencies rose 38 percent last year to the equivalent of 12.7 billion shekels, the Bank of Israel said on Monday.

The central bank said outstanding loans in actual foreign currency rose 24.2 percent to 47.9 billion shekels at the end of the year while direct borrowing from overseas grew 14.7 percent to 13.9 billion shekels.
Analysts said the big rise in foreign currency-linked credits was due to high domestic interest rates.
Inflation-indexed borrowing in shekels rose 24.2 percent in the year to 95.8 billion shekels, while unlinked borrowing grew 15.4 percent to 81.1 billion shekels, the central bank said.

In the meantime, demand deposits grew 8.7 percent to 9.3 billion shekels at year's end. Short-term deposits grew 44 percent to 75.3 billion shekels, which analysts said was in large part due to the public's withdrawing funds from the stock and bond markets last year.

M1 money supply grew 12.3 percent, which a banking source said reflected the influence of the Bank of Israel's restrictive monetary policy. Inflation last year was 10.6 percent, while gross domestic product grew an estimated 4.4 percent, according to the Central Bureau of Statistics.
M2 growth was a sharper 32 percent to 106.9 billion shekels, the bank said.
